2004A16.goal: In a $5\times5$ grid, count the squares (sizes $1$–$5$) that contain the centre cell. For each size, count positions whose span covers row $3$ and column $3$.

tools.name: Independent row and column ranges
tools.why: A $k\times k$ square covers the centre iff both its row span and column span include $3$.

tools.name: Starts covering the middle
tools.why: The start must be between $4-k$ and $3$, within $1..6-k$.

2004A16.approach: Sizes $1,2,3,4,5$ give $1,2,3,2,1$ valid starts per direction. Square them and add: $1+4+9+4+1$.

check.q: How many $3\times3$ squares contain the centre?

2004A16.bridge: Count valid starts per direction and square.
2004A16.shortcut: Row-start counts $1,2,3,2,1$ are symmetric; square and sum.
2004A16.recognize: Squares containing a given cell: count horizontal and vertical placements separately.

2004A17.goal: Brenda and Sally start opposite on a track of length $L$, running toward each other. First meeting after Brenda runs $100$; next after Sally runs $150$ more. We want $L$. Between meetings, together they cover one full lap.

tools.name: Combined distances
tools.why: Approaching each other around the circle.

tools.name: Constant speeds
tools.why: Twice the combined distance takes twice the time.

2004A17.approach: The second leg is twice the first in combined distance, so Brenda runs $200$ in it. Then $L=200+150=350$.

steps.title: Brenda between meetings
steps.explain: Combined $L$ vs. $\tfrac L2$: twice the time, so Brenda runs $2\cdot100=200$.

check.q: If time doubles at constant speed, distance does what?

2004A17.bridge: Double Brenda's first distance, add Sally's second distance.
2004A17.recognize: Runners meeting repeatedly in opposite directions: each meeting adds one lap of combined distance.

2004A18.goal: AP $9,9+d,9+2d$; then $9,11+d,29+2d$ is geometric. We want the smallest possible third GP term. Use the GP condition (middle squared = product of ends).
traps: Adding $2$ and $20$ to the wrong terms.
2004A18.recognize: AP turned into GP: write the AP with $d$, apply $b^2=ac$.

2004A19.goal: A stripe of horizontal width $3$ winds around a silo of height $80$. We want its area. Unroll the cylinder: the stripe becomes a parallelogram.

tools.name: Unrolling
tools.fact: \text{the lateral surface is a flat rectangle}

2004A19.approach: Slicing the stripe into horizontal strips, each has width $3$, stacked over height $80$ (shear doesn't change area). Area $=3\cdot80$.

steps.title: Unroll
steps.explain: Flattened, the stripe is a slanted band; every horizontal cross-section has length $3$.

check.q: Does the number of revolutions change the area?
check.why: Cavalieri: same width at every height.

solution: Unrolled, the stripe has horizontal width $3$ at every height.
2004A19.recognize: Stripes on cylinders: unroll; Cavalieri gives width × height.

2004A20.goal: In unit square $ABCD$, $E$ on $AD$ and $F$ on $CD$ make $\triangle BEF$ equilateral. We want $\tfrac{[DEF]}{[ABE]}$. Symmetry gives $DE=DF=x$.

check.q: What is the positive root of $x^2+2x-2=0$?

2004A20.bridge: Use symmetry, equate $BE$ and $EF$, compute the ratio.
2004A20.shortcut: Angle chasing: $\angle ABE=15^\circ$; ratios of $15^\circ$-triangles give $2$ quickly.
2004A20.recognize: Equilateral triangle inscribed from a square's corner: symmetric, with $15^\circ$ angles.

2004A21.goal: Concentric circles of radii $3,2,1$ and two lines through the centre at acute angle $\theta$. The shaded region (acute sectors of the inner disk and outer ring, obtuse sectors of the middle ring) is $\tfrac8{13}$ of the unshaded region. We want $\theta$.

steps.title: Shaded area
steps.explain: Inner disk: $\theta$. Middle ring ($4-1=3$): $3(\pi-\theta)$. Outer ring ($9-4=5$): $5\theta$. Total $3\pi+3\theta$.

check.q: What is the area of a ring between radii $2$ and $3$ in a sector of angle $\alpha$ (radians)?

2004A21.bridge: Write the shaded area in $\theta$ and match the given fraction.
traps: Using degrees in the sector formula.
2004A21.recognize: Sectors across concentric rings: area $\tfrac\alpha2(R^2-r^2)$ for each ring.

2004A22.goal: Square side $2$, semicircle on $AB$ inside; the tangent from $C$ hits $AD$ at $E$. We want $CE$. Both $CB$ and $EA$ are also tangent to the semicircle.

tools.name: Equal tangents
tools.fact: \text{tangent lengths from a point are equal}
tools.why: $CB$ and $EA$ touch the circle at $B$ and $A$.

check.q: Why is $CB$ tangent to the semicircle?
check.why: A line perpendicular to a radius at its endpoint.

traps: Ignoring that the sides are tangents.
Using coordinates for the tangent point (slow).
2004A22.recognize: Tangent segments crossing a figure with tangent sides: add equal tangent lengths.

2004A23.goal: Circle $D$ contains circles $A$ (radius $1$, through $D$'s centre) and congruent $B,C$ (radius $r$), all mutually tangent. We want $r$. Use coordinates with $D$'s centre at $O$.

tools.name: Radius of $D$
tools.why: $A$ passes through $O$ and is internally tangent: diameter of $A$ = radius of $D$.

tools.name: Tangency distances
tools.why: $B,C$ are symmetric across line $OA$ and touch each other.

opts: B\text{ and }C\text{ touch on the axis}
check.why: Mirror images that touch meet on the line of symmetry.

2004A23.bridge: Coordinates with the symmetry line as an axis.
2004A23.shortcut: Descartes' circle theorem also gives $\tfrac89$ quickly.
2004A23.recognize: Mutually tangent circles inside a circle: coordinates + distance equations.

2004A24.goal: $f(1)=1$, $f(2n)=n\,f(n)$. We want $f(2^{100})$. Apply the rule repeatedly along powers of $2$.
2004A24.recognize: Recursions on powers of $2$: track the exponent.

2004A25.goal: Three touching unit spheres rest on a plane; a radius-$2$ sphere sits on top. We want the height of its top. The centres form a triangular pyramid.

tools.name: Centroid distance
tools.why: Circumradius of an equilateral triangle with side $2$.

tools.name: Vertical rise
tools.why: Big centre is $1+2=3$ from each small centre.

2004A25.approach: Small centres at height $1$, forming an equilateral triangle of side $2$. The big centre is above the centroid at height $1+\sqrt{9-\tfrac43}=1+\tfrac{\sqrt{69}}3$. Add radius $2$.

check.q: How high are the small centres?

solution: Small centres: height $1$, triangle side $2$, circumradius $\tfrac2{\sqrt3}$.
2004A25.shortcut: Stacked spheres: horizontal offset from the centroid, vertical by Pythagoras.
traps: Forgetting the small centres are at height $1$.
2004A25.recognize: Spheres resting on spheres: work with the centres.
